newsitem.title: INDIA: India coalition says Chidambaram to retain his job.
newsitem.headline: India coalition says Chidambaram to retain his job.

text.p: India's United Front coalition said on Sunday it was confident that outgoing Finance Minister P. Chidambaram would retain his job in a new government and push the 1997/98 budget through parliament.
"I am confident that Finance Minister P. Chidambaram will pilot the Finance Bill through parliament," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy told a news conference.
Asked how certain he was that Chidambaram, whose Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) party has vowed not to join the new government, would remain finance minister, Reddy said: "One hundred percent."
"The budgetary proposals, barring a few amendments, will be adopted," he said.

Parliament is due to meet on Monday to consider the 1997/98 (April-March) budget, containing a battery of tax-cutting and tariff-reduction proposals that Chidambaram presented in February and which have delighted markets.
Earlier on Sunday, Chidambaram refused to discuss the budget. Asked to comment on its fate, he told Reuters: "I'm not going to talk about it. You should ask the new government."
Chidambaram's angry withdrawal from the government raised questions over the future of his budget but analysts said it would clear parliament even without his guiding hand.

"By and large, the Finance Bill as proposed by Chidambaram will go through parliament, perhaps with some minor amendments, and we can celebrate the depoliticisation of the budget," said Charan Wadhva of New Delhi's Centre for Policy Research.
Prime minister-designate Inder Kumar Gujral was due to be sworn in on Monday and to face a confidence vote on Tuesday.
With the support of 140 votes from its ally, the Congress party, the United Front's 178 lawmakers should easily push the budget through the 542-member lower house of parliament.
Economist Sanjaya Baru said Gujral might curtail a proposed reduction in taxes on business and higher income groups to appease communist members of the coalition who backed his appointment.
Minutes after Gujral was nominated as the coalition's new leader on Saturday, the TMC announced it would pull out of the government but continue to support the alliance in parliament.

TMC leader G.K. Moopanar had been considered a favourite for the job, and the powerful regional group's decision to withdraw could merely be a tactic to press Gujral into luring party representatives back with cabinet posts, analysts said.
"I am absolutely confident that the United Front will be able to prevail upon the TMC to join the government eventually," spokesman Reddy said.
Gujral said he planned to finalise a council of ministers by Monday.
